column1: # How the figures group the wheat pathogens into rows. AUTHORED, not derived.
# `group` is the disease type a wheat pathologist would name, which is what the figures band
# rows by; `group_order` fixes the band order and runs broadly from the obligate biotrophs to
# the necrotrophs, which is also roughly Basidiomycota -> Leotiomycetes -> Dothideomycetes ->
# Sordariomycetes. `class` and `lifestyle` are recorded so the grouping can be switched to
# either without re-curating, and because lifestyle bears on how a detection is read: an
# obligate biotroph cannot be present as dead deposited material and still be transcribing.
# `collapse` marks a genus drawn as ONE row rather than one row per species, because its
# species-level calls are a single organism spread over near-identical references. Only
# Alternaria qualifies and the evidence is measured, not asserted: within a run its species
# are called at a median coverage CV of 0.24 against 0.63 to 0.92 for every other genus, and
# a run calling it calls a median of twelve species at once. The plot RE-MEASURES this at
# draw time and warns if an uncollapsed genus starts behaving the same way, so the decision
# is audited by the data rather than frozen here.
# A taxon drawn by a figure and missing here is a hard error, never a silent drop.
# The GENUS row. A collapsed genus is placed explicitly, not inherited from whichever of its
# species sorts first: alphabetically that was Alternaria alternata, which put the cluster in
# the Leaf blotch band and implied the calls resolve to a wheat pathogen. They do not. The
# cluster is dominated by infectoria-group saprotrophs and cannot be resolved to species at
# all, so it sits with the saprotrophs and the caption says the genus also contains wheat
